claim: The SCOURGE consortium conducted a genome-wide association study (GWAS) for COVID-19 hospitalization in admixed Americans, comprising a total of 4702 hospitalized cases.
source: In this second study nested in the SCOURGE consortium, we conducted a genome-wide association study (GWAS) for COVID-19 hospitalization in admixed Americans, comprising a total of 4702 hospitalized cases recruited by SCOURGE and seven other participating studies in the COVID-19 Host Genetic Initiative.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the study design, sample size, and composition in the abstract.

claim: Two novel loci (BAZ2B and DDIAS) were first discovered in Latin American populations.
source: We identified four genome-wide significant associations, two of which constitute novel loci and were first discovered in Latin American populations (BAZ2B and DDIAS).
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the discovery of two novel loci in Latin American populations.

claim: A trans-ethnic meta-analysis revealed a novel cross-population risk locus in CREBBP.
source: A trans-ethnic meta-analysis revealed another novel cross-population risk locus in CREBBP.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the discovery of a novel locus in CREBBP through trans-ethnic meta-analysis.

claim: More than 50 loci have been associated with COVID-19 susceptibility, hospitalization, and severity using genome-wide association studies.
source: To date, more than 50 loci associated with COVID-19 susceptibility, hospitalization, and severity have been identified using genome-wide association studies (GWAS) (Kanai et al., 2023; Pairo-Castineira et al., 2023).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The COVID-19 Host Genetics Initiative has made significant efforts to augment the power to identify disease loci by recruiting individuals from diverse populations.
source: The COVID-19 Host Genetics Initiative (HGI) has made significant efforts (Niemi et al., 2021) to augment the power to identify disease loci by recruiting individuals from diverse populations and conducting a trans-ancestry meta-analysis.
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to Niemi et al., 2021.

claim: The lack of genetic diversity and a focus on cases of European ancestries still predominate in COVID-19 genetic studies.
source: Despite this, the lack of genetic diversity and a focus on cases of European ancestries still predominate in the studies (Popejoy and Fullerton, 2016; Sirugo et al., 2019).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to published studies on genetic diversity in research.

claim: Trans-ancestry meta-analyses may fail to identify risk variants that have larger effects on particular underrepresented populations.
source: In addition, while trans-ancestry meta-analyses are a powerful approach for discovering shared genetic risk variants with similar effects across populations (Li and Keating, 2014), they may fail to identify risk variants that have larger effects on particular underrepresented populations.
evidence: The statement is supported by citation to Li and Keating, 2014, and represents a logical inference about the limitations of trans-ancestry meta-analyses.

claim: Genetic disease risk has been shaped by the particular evolutionary history of populations and environmental exposures.
source: Genetic disease risk has been shaped by the particular evolutionary history of populations and environmental exposures (Rosenberg et al., 2010).
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to Rosenberg et al., 2010.

claim: A DOCK2 gene variant is associated with severe COVID-19 in East Asians.
source: Literature examples of this in COVID-19 severity include a DOCK2 gene variant in East Asians (Namkoong et al., 2022) and frequent loss-of-function variants in IFNAR1 and IFNAR2 genes in Polynesian and Inuit populations, respectively (Bastard et al., 2022; Duncan et al., 2022).
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to Namkoong et al., 2022.

claim: Frequent loss-of-function variants in IFNAR1 and IFNAR2 genes are found in Polynesian and Inuit populations, respectively.
source: Literature examples of this in COVID-19 severity include a DOCK2 gene variant in East Asians (Namkoong et al., 2022) and frequent loss-of-function variants in IFNAR1 and IFNAR2 genes in Polynesian and Inuit populations, respectively (Bastard et al., 2022; Duncan et al., 2022).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to Bastard et al., 2022 and Duncan et al., 2022.

claim: The SCOURGE consortium recruited COVID-19 patients between March and December 2020 from hospitals across Spain and from March 2020 to July 2021 in Latin America.
source: The Spanish Coalition to Unlock Research on Host Genetics on COVID-19 (SCOURGE) recruited COVID-19 patients between March and December 2020 from hospitals across Spain and from March 2020 to July 2021 in Latin America (https://www.scourge-covid.org).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the recruitment timeline and locations.

claim: A first GWAS of COVID-19 severity among Spanish patients of European descent revealed novel disease loci.

claim: The SCOURGE Latin American cohort included 1608 hospitalized cases and 1887 controls.

claim: The GWAS meta-analysis revealed genome-wide significant associations at four risk loci.

evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of significant loci and references Table 2 and Figure 2 showing the results.

claim: The sentinel variant rs13003835 in BAZ2B is associated with an increased risk of COVID-19 hospitalization (OR=1.20, 95% CI = 1.12–1.27, p=3.66 × 10–8).

evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the association statistics for rs13003835 and references Figure 3.

source: This association was not previously reported in any GWAS of COVID-19 published to date.

claim: rs13003835 did not reach significance (p=0.972) in the COVID-19 HGI trans-ancestry meta-analysis including the five population groups.

evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the p-value for this variant in the HGI trans-ancestry meta-analysis and cites Kanai et al., 2023.

claim: The sentinel variant rs77599934 in DDIAS is associated with the risk of COVID-19 hospitalization (OR = 2.27, 95% CI = 1.70–3.04, p=2.26 × 10–8).

evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the association statistics for rs77599934 and references Figure 3.

evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the association statistics for rs2601183.

claim: DDIAS is known as damage-induced apoptosis suppressor gene and has been linked to DNA damage repair mechanisms.
source: DDIAS, known as damage-induced apoptosis suppressor gene, is itself a plausible candidate gene. It has been linked to DNA damage repair mechanisms: research has shown that depletion of DDIAS leads to an increase in ATM phosphorylation and the formation of p53-binding protein (53BP1) foci, a known biomarker of DNA double-strand breaks, suggesting a potential role in double-strand break repair (Brunette et al., 2019).
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to Brunette et al., 2019.

claim: Infection by SARS-CoV-2 triggered the phosphorylation of ATM kinase and inhibited repair mechanisms, causing the accumulation of DNA damage.
source: Interestingly, a study found that infection by SARS-CoV-2 also triggered the phosphorylation of ATM kinase and inhibited repair mechanisms, causing the accumulation of DNA damage (Gioia et al., 2023).
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to Gioia et al., 2023.

claim: DDIAS has been proposed as a potential biomarker for lung cancer after finding that it interacts with STAT3 in lung cancer cells, regulating IL-6.
source: This gene has also been proposed as a potential biomarker for lung cancer after finding that it interacts with STAT3 in lung cancer cells, regulating IL-6 (Im et al., 2020; Im et al., 2023) and thus mediating inflammatory processes, while another study determined that its blockade inhibited lung cancer cell growth (Won et al., 2014).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to Im et al., 2020, Im et al., 2023, and Won et al., 2014.
